data.title: HIP-3: An Expensive Admission Ticket and an Indispensable Moat
data.description:
Author: Mario Chow @ IOSG

Ten teams have registered their own perpetual markets on Hyperliquid, most of which have locked approximately $40M of HYPE for this purpose. One of them accounted for 97.8% of the trading volume and recently experienced a 44% drop in a single month. This article aims to answer what the other nine teams bought, using figures taken entirely from on-chain data, not official announcements.

 与 clearinghouseState{dex}. "30 days" refers to the full UTC calendar days from August 15 to September 13, 2026; "previous 30 days" refers to July 16 to August 14; "7 days" refers to September 7 to 13. HYPE is calculated at $79.73. The routing data in Section 7 is taken from Flowscan because the transaction volume of builder code cannot be aggregated from the public API. HIP-3 has once again become a minority in Hyperliquid. The market for builder deployments accounted for 25.8% of perpetual trading volume over 30 days, compared to 57.1% last month. This change is primarily due to the denominator: core market trading volume more than doubled, while HIP-3 itself declined. The leader is contracting. Trade[XYZ]'s 30-day trading volume was $64.60 billion, a 44.2% decrease month-over-month. The 7-day average volume dropped from a high of $5.36 billion/day in early August to $2.01 billion/day. About half of this decline corresponds to a decrease in real-market trading volume in the storage and AI sectors, while the other half is attributed to the platform itself. It hasn't outperformed the core order book on any single day since August 18th. Entropy (io) led for a full week in a head-to-head market before giving it back. Its share on Nebius has followed a trajectory of 8.7%, 53.1%, and 20.4% for three consecutive weeks, while its trading volume has also declined for three consecutive weeks. A contrarian signal is in open interest: open interest has risen against the trend by 37% to $51.4M. Settlement assets remain the lifeline, with the record still showing a 6-to-6 ratio. All venues using non-USDC stablecoins for settlement have ceased trading; those still operating use USDC. Asset listings are failing to hold. At the current auction reserve price, one asset unit is approximately $39,900. Buying the entire Paragon online market would only cost around $1.04M, equivalent to two weeks' worth of transaction fees from Trade[XYZ]. No one is competing on price. All stock-related venues are running on deployerFeeScale = 1.0 with Growth Mode, with tested rates of 0.427 bp for Trade[XYZ] and 0.400 bp for Entropy. All venues except the leading one, regardless of their success or failure, combined, will only earn a total of $747,000 in deployment fees over their entire lifespan.

Ten Deployers Present

▲ Daily trading volume of Trade[XYZ], and all the challengers below it. The vertical axis scales of the two charts differ by approximately 100 times.

Ten Deployers Present

“Number of trades” is the sum of the 'n' and 'n' fields from the daily candlestick chart within the window. The public API cannot derive the number of independent traders.

Historically, only ten perpetual DEXs have registered, and there has never been an eleventh. Four are trading, five have stopped, and one has never opened.

In history, only ten have registered perpetual DEXs, and there has never been an eleventh. Four are trading, five have stopped, and one has never opened.

Trade[XYZ] accounted for 97.8% of HIP-3 trading volume over the past 30 days and 97.6% over the past 7 days. The challengers' situation can be summarized in a few words. Entropy traded $1.03 billion in 26 days across six online markets, relying on its self-built oracle rather than an asset list. It's the only venue that truly led in markets where the leading oracle also provided quotes. Paragon is the only challenger whose order book looks like an order book, with 26 online markets and a well-distributed tail. Even with Trade[XYZ] buying five of its assets at once, it still rose 49.9% that month. Markets by Kinetiq bought 23 assets, with 95% of the volume concentrated in two perpetual indexes. HyENA is finished: the entire market was delisted, open positions went to zero, and it earned $33,414 over its lifetime.

HIP-3's share, and why it is easily misunderstood

▲ The percentage of HIP-3 in Hyperliquid perpetual trading volume, calculated daily.

What we really need to look at is the absolute volume, and the absolute volume is deteriorating. Trade[XYZ]'s 30-day trading volume was $64.60B, a 44.2% decrease compared to the previous month. The 7-day average volume dropped from $5.36B/day in early August to $2.01B/day, and its own order book retreated by 62%. The largest market, SK Hynix, fell to $8.50B. Both legs of the declining percentage are real.

What we really need to look at is the absolute volume, and the absolute volume is deteriorating.

The following section will explain that the main issue with HIP-3 is not competition. The main reason for the decline in trading volume is the quieting of the storage sector, not a loss of market share. Interpreting the 44% drop directly as "the leader is losing" is the easiest explanation, but the data doesn't support it. The verification method is simple: if the decline was due to competition, we should see that the underlying asset itself is trading normally, only the portion captured by Trade[XYZ] has decreased. What actually happened was that the underlying asset itself quieted down. There was no selling. Compared to the peak trading volume in early August, the prices in every major market today are higher.

What really collapsed was how far these targets could go in a day, while the trading volume of the venue almost followed suit.

Kinetiq is the control group. The only operator that survived after shutting down did so by cutting off the USDH venue and relaunching the exact same index product on USDC. Historical trading volume is unpredictable: Dreamcash traded $19.51 billion, more than the entire June batch combined, yet it still shut down. Entropy entered in August with more funds than any previous entrant, showing no hesitation in choosing USDC.

What truly determines the settlement asset, and what is it not?

It's natural to interpret the sweep of USDC as an arrangement of the protocol, but Hyperliquid's own documentation says the opposite.

Under Aligned Quote Assets v2 (launched on USDC in late August, with Coinbase as the treasury deployer and Circle as the technical deployer), approximately 90% of USDC's cost-adjusted reserve earnings on Hyperliquid are distributed to the protocol and go into the Assistance Fund. Interest is calculated in 30-day increments, with payments made 8 days after the end of each increment. Therefore, the first payment will be due in early October, and none has been received yet. What AQAv2 explicitly does not do is precisely to favor HIP-3. The documentation is very clear: there are no preferential treatments in terms of transaction fees or volume inclusion, and other denominated assets continue to be supported on HIP-3 perpetual bonds. The fee advantages belong to AQAv1, which offers lower taker fees, higher maker rebates, and higher trading volume for collateralized assets. USDC is not in AQAv1 and structurally cannot be included because that tier requires stablecoins to be exclusively owned by Hyperliquid. The real privileges offered by AQAv2 point to the perpetual operation of event contracts and validators, and this will have to wait for a future upgrade, which is not the market measured in this article. Therefore, the settlement of assets is determined by liquidity and a company-level action, not by fee design. USDH will cease operations on July 17, 2026, and holders will redeem their assets at a 1:1 ratio for USDC. Coinbase will acquire its brand assets and become the treasury deployer for USDC. Today, USDC accounts for 98.3% of the stablecoin supply on Hyperliquid, USDT 1.2%, and the remainder for feUSD, USDe, and USDH is approximately 0.1% each. A venue settling with other assets isn't losing out on fees. It's essentially asking its traders to leave the only pool with sufficient depth. Let's estimate the size of AQAv2, assuming no official figures have ever been released. USDC on Hyperliquid is $6.77bn, with an SOFR of approximately 3.6%. Assuming a 90% cut, this roughly points to around $200M per year. Third-party estimates based on $5bn fall between $135M and $160M. What's uncertain externally is the cost adjustment in the AQA interest rate, which is based on an oracle reported by validators. Its performance isn't publicly disclosed, so every figure here is calculated, not actually measured. HyENA added a second mechanism. Because it listed crypto assets, it was excluded from Growth Mode, resulting in a price of approximately 5 basis points on the same asset, while its core token price was around 3 basis points, with even worse trading quality. It spent approximately $0.88M on its asset base, earning a total of $33,414 over its lifetime. A standstill doesn't equal exit. HyENA has been delisted from all 25 markets, with open positions reduced to zero, but its staked assets remain at 508,915 HYPE, approximately $40.6M, and no withdrawals have been initiated in the past twelve days. Felix and Dreamcash have both withdrawn their full staked amount, now showing a zero balance, and Ventures only has 7,967 remaining. A platform that delists the entire market but keeps $40M staked on-chain either has slow liquidation processes or is reserving that deployment space for something else. The exact cause of Ventures' demise deserves a separate discussion, as the next generation of products is designed around this issue. Insufficient liquidity is merely a symptom; the underlying mechanism lies in the funding rate: pre-IPO perpetual tokens lacked a convergence anchor, and funding rates once reached approximately 8,700% annualized, resulting in the liquidation of long positions regardless of the marked price. Entropy capped its annualized funding rate at around 10% and settled to its own marked price in TWAP, rather than chasing an external price. Its overall contract design can be read as a checklist of fixes for the specific causes of Ventures' demise. When looking at any pre-IPO listing, first look at the funding rates and settlement design, then look at the asset list. The order book structure of Trade[XYZ], and why it doesn't list OpenAI. (Image of the image: https://img.jinse.com.cn/7509987_image3.png, title: 7509987, alt: rNs7l9BiXaTNAI3Fspwwv9XMXdfeuQNK5hC2pAhd.jpeg) ▲ The market with the highest trading volume for Trade[XYZ] in the past 30 days. The top ten markets account for 66.7% of the total market capitalization, and even the bottom ten outside the top six account for $32.4 billion. Nvidia accounts for 3.5%. Apple, Tesla, Alphabet, and Microsoft combined account for 3.3%, only a quarter of SK Hynix's share. The American giants that the standard narrative of tokenized US stocks loves to talk about are not in this business. Trade[XYZ] actually operates a 24/7 marketplace for trading storage and AI capital expenditures, plus crude oil, metals, and index products: Korean and Japanese semiconductors, a synthetic DRAM index, SpaceX, its own XYZ100 basket, and a licensed S&P 500. Its territory is the kind of assets that native crypto traders can't access elsewhere at 3 a.m. This is precisely the territory Entropy chose to attack, targeting SanDisk and Nebius, not Apple. The most intuitive answer, saying it avoids unlisted companies, is wrong. Pre-IPO is actually one of its better businesses. SpaceX alone generated $2.80 billion in 30 days, accounting for 4.3% of the market, ranking ninth. Following that are Unitree ($511M), Changxin Memory ($317M), Zhipu ($156M), MiniMax ($92M), SHEIN ($27M), and Yangtze Memory Technologies (YMTC) is already registered and awaiting issuance. These names have one thing in common: they all have observable secondary market prices and known share capital. SpaceX regularly makes tender offers, providing a clear price per share; these Chinese companies have active pre-IPO grey markets in mainland China, and their share capital can be obtained from business registration information and financing rounds. Therefore, this venue can treat them like any other asset, quoting prices per share. OpenAI and Anthropic, however, do not. Their secondary transactions are all within SPVs, dealing with the claim to fund units and negotiating an overall valuation, not a specific price per share. Insisting on quoting per share is like creating a denominator. The bottleneck lies here; it's a matter of pricing convention, not a matter of willingness. Entropy's solution is to simply not quote per share, but rather the company itself. One contract = $1 billion market capitalization. Based on the current median price, Anthropic is close to $2.17 billion, and OpenAI is close to $1.53 billion. But this doesn't constitute a moat. A leading company can easily add a market capitalization-valued asset to its portfolio for around $39,900. Moreover, its roadmap points elsewhere: it has 16 registered but not yet activated assets, with uranium, aluminum, the US dollar index, VIX, corn, wheat, TTF, South Korean won, Indian Nifty, Brazilian Ibovespa, Ibiden, and KSTR in the pipeline, plus Yangtze Memory and H100. This is macroeconomics and commodities, not cutting-edge AI labs. One structural detail is worth remembering. Trade[XYZ] does not have an oracleUpdater configured, meaning it uses its own deployment key to push the marked price; while Entropy and Felix both point to the same third-party updater: 0x94757f8d…. Entropy has publicly stated that RedStone is its price data source for the Anthropic market, which explains why two unrelated marketplaces share an update address, although this address is not tagged on-chain. Building your own oracle is fine for assets with reference prices, but the nature changes when the marked price must be "constructed," and constructing marked prices is precisely the business Entropy has chosen.

Head-to-head confrontation, and the week Entropy led

▲ Nebius' weekly trading volume, and Entropy's share within it.

Currently, nine assets are active simultaneously on two HIP-3 venues.

Each firm no longer occupies a separate, non-overlapping order book; overlapping listings are now the norm for any name worth listing twice. The competition for a spot reduces market share, not the order book itself. Trade[XYZ] had registered five core Paragon assets but didn't use them. On August 18th, all five were opened in one day, and today it's leading in all five. Filling this gap cost about three days' worth of commission income, but it was all done in one afternoon. Whether those targets were a deterrent or were already in the queue for listing couldn't be determined from the on-chain data. What could be determined was the outcome. Four weeks later, Paragon still held 20% to 25% of four of the five, and its overall trading volume increased by 49.9% that month. The Unique Tree (UK) algorithm best illustrates this mechanism: Trade[XYZ]'s UK order book was approximately 11 times that of Paragon, while Paragon only accounted for 8.2% of this pair, yet Paragon's own UK trading volume nearly doubled during the same period. The leader didn't steal volume from the challenger; it expanded the market around the challenger. Entering a market and owning a market are two different things. Entropy led on Nebius for a week, then gave it back. For one week, Entropy's Nebius trading volume did indeed exceed that of Trade[XYZ], something the HIP-3 challenger had never achieved before. The following week, the leading Nebius order book rose 61%, while Entropy fell 63%, and the challenger returned to one-fifth of the pair. SanDisk tells the same story, only more quietly: Entropy's share has hovered around 13% in recent weeks, totaling 8.5% over the entire 30 days. So this lead is real, and it really only lasted a week. The honest way to read it is: Entropy has proven it can enter a market where a leading stock is actively quoting, but it hasn't proven it can hold onto it. Its total volume has fallen for three consecutive weeks, from $417M to $254M. A contrarian signal comes from inventory. While weekly volume has fallen 39% from its peak, Entropy's open interest has actually increased by 37% to $51.4M, with Anthropic alone accounting for $29.9M. The transactions generated by inflated volume will be repeatedly offset, leaving no inventory. Therefore, while the trading volume declines, the open interest continues to accumulate, indicating real holdings rather than idle trading. These two facts are contradictory; what we should really focus on is the tension itself, not any single number. The volume here needs to be discounted. Entropy doesn't have a token and hasn't confirmed an airdrop, but its backend already shows the `pointsM` parameter, and its own leaderboard page says "coming soon." Therefore, some of the traffic is generating anticipation rather than using the product, and these two aspects cannot be separated from external factors. The scale is also a factor: Entropy earns approximately $1.0B per month, while Trade[XYZ] earns $64.6B, representing 1.6% of the leader. It won specific battles, not just the category itself. Its registered, yet-to-be-listed assets reveal its next move. Entropy holds EWY, SBE, TCNT, and a DRAM index. The DRAM index is Trade[XYZ]'s fourth largest product, while EWY represents South Korea. The next battle seems poised to directly target the leader's core territory, rather than seeking another uncontested pre-IPO name. Two counting rules: Only online order book is counted. HIP-3 deployers often register their targets well in advance. These targets will return the oracle's `markPx`, but `m` will be null, `i` will be true, `sDeli` will be true, `sted` will be true, open interest will be zero, and there will be no candlestick history. Trade[XYZ] has 16, mkts 19, Paragon 9, and Entropy 4. HyENA's 25 are a different matter; they were enabled and then disabled. The code string is not equal to the target. para:STX is Seagate, mid-price 799; the core board's S ...

Economics: Costs of a Venue, Revenue Across the Entire Level

Nobody's competing on price because rates have bottomed out

Everything comes down to two parameters for each asset, both of which are publicly available in metaAndAssetCtxs:growthMode  anddeployerFeeScale. The total fee is base × (1 + s), where base is the standard perpetual fee rate table, and s is the deployer coefficient, which can be set from 0 to 3.00, capped at 1.00 in Growth Mode. The deployer takes s / (1 + s), so when s = 1.00, half is taken. Growth Mode further cuts the total fee by at least 90%, provided that the market must not overlap with the perpetual market operated by validators, thus excluding crypto assets and crypto indices.

All stock-based venues have independently converged to the same configuration: maximum revenue sharing for deployers, and Growth Mode enabled. Entropy entered the market with differentiated products and venture capital, without attempting to drive down prices. The only venue not included in this configuration is the one that recently ceased trading.

Even without any aggregator, the revenue sharing for deployers can be accurately calculated.

Even without any aggregator, the revenue sharing for deployers can be accurately calculated.

Transaction fee income is deposited in the branch account of the fee receiving address: The unspent balance can be read by including the `dex` field. Transfers appear in `userNonFundingLedgerUpdates`, with the format `sourceDex` equal to the branch name's `send`. The transfers are very irregular, so it's necessary to measure between transfers. Trade[XYZ] has accumulated $1,380,592 since the transfer on August 27th, corresponding to a trading volume of $32.30B, or 0.427 bp, approximately $79,000 per day. Entropy has never transferred any funds, so its accumulated fees can be directly read: $1.036B in trading volume corresponding to $41,468, or 0.400 bp.

Two expenditures, completely different in nature

Staking is the scariest number, but it will come back. Nobody takes this money. It's delegated to validators, constantly generating staking rewards, which are returned as is upon exit. ... It is locked for at least 183 days from deployment and can be slashed by weighted validator votes for malicious market manipulation (such as pushing bad oracle prices). It can also be slashed during the 7-day unstaking queue, so a clean exit takes at least 190 days. Felix and Dreamcash both recovered their full amounts, and their current readings are zero. Currently outstanding staked assets: Entropy 500,973, Paragon 500,712, HyENA 508,915 (trading suspended but not yet unstaking), Kinettiq 588,489 (one stake covering both km and mkts), Trade[XYZ] 500,488 plus 500,269 on another address. ABCDEx has only 1,004 HYPEs, which have never been staked. The money in asset slots is the one nobody talks about, and it's truly irrecoverable. The first three assets on any perpetual DEX are free. After that, each additional market must be purchased with HYPE in a 31-hour Dutch auction. The opening price is twice the previous transaction price, linearly decreasing to a floor price of 500 HYPE. The auction on September 14th opened at the floor price of 500 and ended at 500, so one asset slot is approximately $39,900. Demand for asset slots has decreased compared to the transaction price of 582 HYPE a week ago. The last column is the key point. Trade[XYZ] can pay off all the bills in about eight weeks of fees. Every challenger except Entropy took longer than HIP-3 existed; and Entropy only survived because it bought seven asset classes instead of thirty. Time will continue to amplify this asymmetry. Pausing a market is free and reversible; paid asset slots can be frozen and reopened, which is how "pending listings" are generated. Reserve slots are accumulated based on historical deployments, using the formula: 7 + 0.2 × (number of past auction deployments). Therefore, Trade[XYZ] has approximately 30 slots available immediately, while new entrants only have 7. Venues opening today with plans for 20 markets can list 10 at once, with the rest having to queue in auctions, taking at least 31 hours per market. Entropy's solution is to avoid this pace: it only listed five markets and then made each one count. The Staking Trap: Except for Entropy, every challenger has earned more from passively staking their entry tickets than they would from operating an exchange. Paragon's lifetime deployment share is $64,281, while a $39.87M stake, at approximately 2.2%, yields about $877,000 per year, roughly 14 times higher. This is hardly a consolation prize. That small return is from newly issued HYPE in the protocol's future emissions reserves, essentially inflation rather than income. It's a dilutionary return on a forced-hold position, denominated in the asset the operator was already passively holding. A 30% drop in HYPE would result in a $12.0M loss on this stake, exceeding ten years' worth of returns. Over the past eight days, HYPE has fallen from $88.37 to $79.73, resulting in a $4.3M reduction in each pledged transaction. Growth Mode has pinned its tested fee rate to around 0.4 bp, with the deployer receiving half. Trade[XYZ] holds 97.8% of the market share, with an annualized trading volume of approximately $786 billion, earning approximately $29M in deployer commissions annually. Rather than calling this the ceiling for the leader, it's more accurate to say that given the current trading volume and fee rate floor, this represents roughly the entire venue's total revenue. Beyond the leading players, at the venue level, there's a stake of approximately $167 million in HYPE today, but each of these companies, regardless of their survival, will only earn a combined $747,000 in deployment fees over their entire lifetime. Looking at this alongside a $14 million seed round, this arithmetic illustrates that, given the current trading volume and fee floor, HIP-3 operators cannot be valued based on transaction fees. The challenger's value can only come from elsewhere: tokens, front-ends, customer relationships, or a product for which the protocol hasn't yet priced it. What truly can be held onto? HIP-3 intentionally commoditized most of what a venue could have protected. Staking can be bought, assets can be bought, the fee floor is shared, and even distribution is shared because every HIP-3 platform can access the same front end. The useful filtering question isn't "Which assets should you list?", because assets can be bought. It's "What do you have that the leader can't buy with a single asset slot?". Of all the venues operating on HIP-3, only one has a clear answer to this question, and its answer is an oracle and a settlement design, not an asset list. Entropy is an exception, and it's worth stating precisely because the answer isn't in the assets themselves. Founded by researchers and traders from Citadel Securities, Optiver, Millennium, and Polymarket, this strength is evident in two aspects. One is the order book depth from day one, which truly impressed Nebius. The other is its funding rate and settlement design, which reads like a direct response to the demise of Ventuals. Its $14 million seed round was led by Ribbit Capital, whose core focus is retail brokerage and fintech distribution, not DeFi. Ribbit's ambition is to hold customers in its own hands, not to profit from a protocol. A point to note regarding the name: Entropy Advisors, deeply intertwined with Arbitrum DAO, and Entropy, the custodian startup invested in by a16z, are completely different companies. Don't glean any connection to the Hyper Foundation from their names. Considering all of this, the sector still appears somewhat thin. A shrinking company accounted for 97.8% of the trading volume. A group of challengers bet $167M on HYPE, only to receive a combined historical fee of $747,000. The only team that actually knew how to price their tokens had just demonstrated their ability to capture a market for a week, but couldn't hold onto it. A more convenient alternative would be to take the protocol's own half of the fees instead of the operator's half; it avoids lock-up, forfeiture risk, and operational burdens. However, it's still not the bulk of Hyperliquid's perpetual fee base, and it has been proven that HIP-3's share exceeding 50% is an illusion during a crypto lull, not a trend. The routing layer, and the traffic it actually touches. Builder code is the closest thing to a "distribution business" on HIP-3. The frontend tags the orders it issues, earning a builder fee, and there's no margin required. Flowscan counted 819 such tags. The traffic they encounter is indeed minimal. Routed transactions amounted to approximately $52.6 billion, about 9% of HIP-3's all-time total of $587 billion; in the last 30 days, it was about $5.3 billion, equivalent to $66.09 billion, or about 8%. Over 90% of the traffic has no frontend tagging whatsoever, which is exactly what an order book dominated by market makers and API traders should look like. The denominator in the fourth column is the $5.30B of transactions routed entirely by builder codes in the past 30 days, not the $66.09B of HIP-3 transactions. Even with the latter, the largest single transaction, CoinDCX, only accounts for 0.7%. These ten companies in the table collectively account for 59.7% of the routed transactions, and Flowscan counted a total of 819 builder codes, so the last 809 codes account for the remaining 40%. Two things are worth highlighting from this table. First, Entropy's $423M routing volume all occurred in the last 30 days, while its own venues only traded $1.03B during the same period. This means that approximately 40% of the orders came from its own controlled front-end. The retail brokerage ambitions behind Ribbit's round are evident in the data, not just in press releases, and this is a different business than simply being a "deployer." Second, Dreamcash offers a cleaner lesson. Its venues have been dead since July 2nd, with zero readings on its own venues, yet its builder code still routed $17.3M in the last 30 days, totaling $3.54B. The deployment business and the front-end business can be cleanly separated, and only one of them requires $40M to enter. There's an easy pitfall to fall into when it comes to counting on third-party dashboards. Venue rankings are usually based on cumulative trading volume by default, so a venue that shut down months ago can still appear to have a significant share. Dreamcash reads 3.3% of HIP-3 trading volume in the full-time view, but $0 in any recent window. Before citing any share, confirm which window it's calculated from. Therefore, the front-ends that are truly worth monitoring are mostly not the deployment sites. Coinbase announced a simplified perpetual interface within its wallet on September 12th, powered by Hyperliquid, covering crypto, tokenized stocks, and prediction markets, targeting markets outside the US. Kraken's parent company is also in talks to integrate Hyperliquid-related perpetual data into a regulated US venue. Neither of them will pledge that 500,000 HYPE. Conclusion: It's hard to be optimistic about adding another HIP-3 deployment provider. Putting everything together, a new HIP-3 venue faces the following figures: The total HIP-3 trading volume outside the leading provider, over 30 days, is $1.49 billion, annualized to approximately $18.1 billion. Based on the measured 0.400 bp, that's $725,000 in deployment provider revenue to be shared by four venues annually. And these four venues are currently pledging approximately $167 million in HYPE. The same amount, passively pledged at 2.2%, would amount to $3.67 million annually. In other words, the money earned from operating these exchanges is roughly one-fifth of what would have been gained by pledging the same amount of capital. This isn't an untapped market; it's a market already priced close to zero, for reasons that are measurable in previous sections. The asset is priced at $39,900, so nothing can hold; the fee floor is shared, with no room for price reduction; distribution is also shared, and the builder code only receives 9% of the traffic; settlement assets have converged 60/6 to USDC, and AQAv2 explicitly doesn't offer any fee advantage to HIP-3, so the protocol doesn't intend to subsidize this layer. An even greater challenge is the ceiling. With a 97.8% market share and every structural advantage, XYZ only achieved 1.2% actual transaction volume on the nine stocks it quoted, and its relative market share in core storage stocks is still declining. A new entrant faces not a "big leader," but a "small leader that is still getting smaller." The exception remains singular, as previously stated: a right that others cannot buy, an oracle that others cannot create, or a funding rate and settlement design that can survive on thin order books. Entropy is the only one that fits this description, yet it was pushed back after a week's lead. The asset list is not the answer; there are now two independent sets of data pointing to the same thing. What will change this judgment? Entropy can hold its ground in a competitive market for a month instead of a week, and maintain SanDisk's market share instead of hovering around 13%. The accumulation of open interest while trading volume declines is the most noteworthy signal, as it's more reliable than trading volume. Entropy's DRAM index and Korean tokens are launching. These two are directly targeting the core territory of the industry leader, rather than just another pre-IPO name with no competition. The result will be a much cleaner test than Nebius. The token terms will make the equity calculations worthwhile. The transaction fees don't add up, and the token doesn't even exist yet. The pre-IPO sector can continue. Anthropic's market capitalization declined after the first week, and OpenAI opened at $5.3M a day, now it's around $4M. As long as one holds steady, this is a category, not just a launch event. The first payment for AQAv2 will be finalized in early October. That will be the first time we can observe the true scale of the protocol's USDC revenue line, comparing it to the current third-party estimates of $135M to $200M. The fee floor is loosening. Hyperliquid signaled in early August that future upgrades would allow HIP-3 deployers to increase fees by up to 3 times per asset, effectively reversing the Growth Mode discount. No timeline has been provided yet, and every figure in Section 6 is based on the current situation. The permissioned market is taking off. HIP-3*, announced on September 3rd, is an optional on-chain whitelist that allows deployers to restrict which wallets can trade in a particular market. It's described as being geared towards compliance and institutional access, and is currently only available on the testnet. This is the first mechanism that could potentially make "access rights" rather than "assets" a scarce resource. A team emerges with exclusive data or index licenses, and the asset truly has a 24/7 crypto-native demand. This remains the only configuration where the preemptive entry logic completely fails. There is evidence that the leading stock's trading volume cannot withstand the end of Growth Mode. Its measured 0.427 bp is only about one-tenth of what would be charged at the standard rate for the same order book. If this exemption is burdensome, then the leading stock's stability is not as high as the share volume suggests. HyENA's uncollateralization of its 508,915 HYPE shares would confirm that this venue has closed rather than been dormant. Several limitations: The argument of "grabbing a seat" is based on measured share volume, but the motivation is inference. The simultaneous launch of five assets on the same day can also be interpreted as a launch pipeline that just happened to complete on that day. The judgment on Entropy is based solely on 26 days of data. Nebius's lead and subsequent reversal are both weekly readings of a single mid-sized asset, neither of which should be taken as established conclusions. Team background and funding rounds are derived from company announcements and media reports, not verifiable on-chain information. The volatility conclusion in Section 2 is a correlation based on a 45-working-day sample, not a causal decomposition. Trading volume and actual volatility may also be driven by the same factor simultaneously; the most direct candidate is a cooling of overall AI capital expenditure trading. The number of trades is not the same as the number of traders; the public API cannot derive independent traders. Capital return figures are calculated based on HYPE $79.73 and a 2.2% annualized staking rate. The latter is a protocol parameter, not a contractual commitment, and will decrease as the total staking volume increases.

data.title: Grayscale: Can Bitcoin optimize private market portfolios?
data.description:
Author: Zach Pandl, Head of Research at Grayscale; Translated by Shaw, Jinse Finance

The private market has become a standard component of institutional portfolios, providing investors with a source of returns beyond public markets such as stocks and bonds. However, these assets often face a range of common risks. Private equity, venture capital, real estate, and private bonds are all affected by the same underlying factors, including economic growth, financing costs, liquidity, and public market valuation levels.

Bitcoin, on the other hand, offers a completely different source of returns based on its underlying logic.Admittedly, it is still subject to the inherent volatility of market cycles, but its core investment logic lies in its fixed total supply, global accessibility, liquidity, and the growing market demand for the scarcity of native digital assets. As shown in Chart 1, Bitcoin has a low correlation with the private equity market, creating conditions for true risk diversification in private equity portfolios. In fact, even a small allocation can produce significant results. Chart 1 shows that in historical backtesting, adding Bitcoin improves the Sharpe ratio of private equity portfolios. This is because the differentiated return characteristics of Bitcoin and its low correlation with private equity assets are sufficient to offset its own higher volatility. (Note: The Sharpe ratio, also known as the Sharpe index, is a standardized indicator for evaluating fund performance. It is an indicator that comprehensively considers both returns and risks, reflecting the additional return per unit of risk beyond the risk-free rate.) From this perspective, Bitcoin can serve as an optimized supplementary asset in a private equity portfolio: private equity assets offer long-term holding returns and illiquidity premiums, while Bitcoin provides exposure to liquid digital scarcity. **Key Conclusion:** Bitcoin helps optimize private equity portfolios. Historically, even low allocations have improved risk-adjusted returns; pairing long-term private equity holdings with highly liquid, scarce digital assets can improve the overall portfolio's Sharpe ratio. **Chart 1: Historically, allocating Bitcoin has improved private equity portfolio performance.**

data.title: Trump denounces AI panic as a "hoax": Don't kill the goose that lays the golden eggs.
data.description:
Author: Xiao Yanyan, Jinshi Data

US President Trump on Monday again defended the rapid expansion of the AI ​​industry, describing the debate surrounding AI security, data center construction, and federal regulation as a **"hoax."

Trump posted several AI-related posts on Truth Social, one of which stated: "Those who say AI will destroy the world, those who say data centers are harmful to communities, are the same people who not long ago said the world would be destroyed by 'climate change.'"

He then claimed that he was "debunking another hoax," namely the claim that AI will take over and destroy the world, that robots will enter cities and wipe out humanity, and called himself a **"hoax debunker."

Trump also questioned why AI industry leaders were actively requesting government regulation of their industry.

He wrote, "When in business history have we ever seen industry leaders calling for regulation on AI, only to have it forcefully drive them to ruin and bankruptcy?" Regarding the opposition to data center construction, Trump argued that opponents are hindering AI infrastructure development because the US is currently far ahead of other countries in this field. Trump said: "The only reason for the AI/data center boom is that the US is far ahead of all other countries. Don't kill this 'golden goose'!" Trump also stated on Monday that what AI really needs is "a strong and smart (highly intelligent!) president," adding that the US has "more than enough" in this regard. He also warned of a "sick conspiracy" surrounding AI and data centers. Trump had previously emphasized that the US must maintain its AI lead: "Frankly, I want to maintain this position because whoever wins AI wins everything." On Monday, Trump also spoke with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, defending AI and data center construction. He believes both are beneficial to the US economy and downplayed concerns surrounding AI security risks. Trump also predicted that day that artificial intelligence will be "the oil of the next 20 to 25 years—it's bigger than the internet." Huang had previously stated that warnings about the accelerated development of AI could create business for cybersecurity companies. He had Trump plugged into the speakers at a technology summit hosted by the "All In" podcast in Los Angeles. During the event, Trump addressed recent warnings from the tech industry, saying, "Robots aren't going to take over everything. AI isn't going to take over the rest of the world. The whole thing is a hoax." The crowd cheered. Trump also stated, "We have to be a little cautious," but emphasized that this "doesn't mean we're going to shut down an industry." Voices advocating for a "slowdown" are growing within the AI ​​industry. Amid Trump's hardline stance, some of the most influential figures in the AI ​​industry are issuing frequent warnings about the risks. Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, is one of the most prominent figures. Last Saturday, he published an article on his personal blog titled "We Must Slow Down the Frontier," advocating for slowing down the development of cutting-edge AI models to "reduce the risk of serious problems." Amodei suggested that if the slowdown could give the industry an extra year or two before models reach critical capability levels, and use this time to advance alignment research, it would "significantly reduce the risk of serious problems." He also recommended strengthening global coordination among democracies and introducing embedded third-party security assessors. Security concerns are also rising within Anthropic. Former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who recently left the AI ​​industry, warned that the technology could "kill us all before the end of this decade." Coxon also accused OpenAI and Anthropic of "gambling with our lives," saying he fears AI labs are racing to develop systems that may ultimately be uncontrollable. According to a report by MS NOW on Monday, citing three sources familiar with the matter, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman reportedly met with Trump backstage at the Republican Midterm Convention in Dallas last Thursday, following widespread dissemination of Coxon's warnings. Altman himself also signaled caution. He warned that the dazzling pace of AI progress could lead to a "very bad" end, with humanity potentially losing "control over the future and handing it over to AI." Altman also stated on the X platform, "We welcome a federal framework that sets consistent safety requirements for cutting-edge AI." He emphasized that competitive pressures facing the United States "should not be a reason for recklessness." Microsoft has also released a temporary code of conduct, which it plans to adopt when training new AI models. David Sacks, the White House's AI director and a former Trump administration official, refuted the growing AI panic. Following Amodei's call to slow down, he posted on the X platform, urging tech giants to "slow down the frontier themselves." Sacks believes that companies' demands for a slowdown are not necessarily entirely selfless. He pointed out that if a company's products contribute to truly destructive cyberattacks, it could face significant product liability risks. He also stated that the market is already punishing models that behave unpredictably or act without authorization. The Trump administration currently maintains overall support for the rapid development of the AI ​​industry and the construction of data centers in the US to provide computing power for AI. Trump previously stated that the government already possesses "enormous criminal and regulatory powers" against AI companies, and that the government has opposed certain actions by some AI companies and their leaders in the past, and has taken action to stop them, and will continue to do so in the future. In a related post, Trump specifically named Amodei and warned those who believe AI poses an existential risk, saying, "You'll soon find out they're working for people who don't have America's best interests at heart!" Anthropic did not immediately respond to requests for comment regarding Trump's posts. Meanwhile, the conflict between Anthropic and the Trump administration has been ongoing for months. The Pentagon previously flagged Anthropic as a supply chain risk, and the company subsequently sued the government, arguing that the Pentagon's retaliatory actions against its stance on AI safety were illegal. A federal judge recently ruled in favor of Anthropic, finding the government's actions illegal. With the midterm elections approaching, AI regulation still faces obstacles. The controversy surrounding AI regulation is now gradually entering the US domestic political agenda. A Gallup poll released in March showed that nearly half of respondents “strongly oppose” building an AI data center in their area. This opposition is not primarily from the Democratic camp. The same Gallup poll showed that slightly less than 40% of Republican respondents also strongly oppose building data centers. With the November 3 midterm elections approaching, protests surrounding data centers are becoming a source of political pressure for Republicans and some Democrats. However, the likelihood of Congress quickly pushing for AI regulation before the midterm elections remains low. House members will adjourn on Thursday to leave Washington and remain in their respective districts throughout October. House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Republican from Louisiana, downplayed the need for immediate legislation to constrain AI development last Sunday. In an interview with CNN's "State of the Union" program, Johnson stated that if Congress "rushes in" and convenes an emergency meeting to try and regulate AI, the United States will lose the competition, which is a threat to every American. He also told reporters on Monday that Trump is expected to convene a meeting with AI companies as early as this week, possibly at the White House, to discuss the next steps. Vice President Vance stated on Monday that the government needs to "regulate smartly," but is skeptical of AI companies proactively requesting more regulatory safeguards. Vance said, "It feels a little strange to me that so many cutting-edge AI technology companies are coming to the government asking to regulate them." He believes this is "a bit like a Trojan horse." Several regulatory proposals are still under consideration within Congress. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, a Republican from South Dakota, said on Monday that AI regulation needs to strike a balance between innovation and risk control. Thune said, "You need a balance, light-touch regulation. You don't want to stifle innovation, but I think you also want to make sure that more advanced threats can be mitigated." Thune also revealed that he has discussed a bipartisan AI regulatory bill with Minnesota Democratic Senator Amy Klobuchar, which he hopes will be introduced soon. One of the goals of this bill is to prevent AI from causing catastrophic risks such as nuclear disasters and biological weapons. The bill is considered one of the most promising AI regulatory proposals in Congress, but with the November 3 midterm elections approaching, the Trump administration's relatively favorable stance towards the AI ​​industry, and AI companies themselves not yet reaching a consensus on potential regulatory paths, the bill's progress still faces challenges.
