data.title: PONS only 0.9x: Why does HYPE have 29x?
data.description:
Although both DeFi tokens rely on buyback mechanisms for price increases, the market valuations of different tokens are showing a very steep curve.

Note: PE = Circulating Market Capitalization ÷ Annualized Revenue, not the traditional financial statement P/E ratio;

*SKY includes staking yield.

*SKY includes staking yield.

Based on the annualized value calculated by dividing the circulating market capitalization by the revenue of the most recent 7 days, PONS, the platform token of Robinhood's on-chain token launchpad Pons, has a 7-day PE ratio of only 0.9; using the same calculation, the 7-day PE ratio of decentralized exchange Hyperliquid (HYPE) is 29.2. Both are conducting buybacks and burns, yet the ratio differs by more than thirty times. This isn't a question of which is cheaper. These figures put DeFi tokens into a pricing language similar to the stock market: how much money the protocol earns, how much it retains, and how much actually ends up in the tokens—how much the market is willing to pay for this revenue is what truly determines the valuation. Buybacks are no longer a plus. First, let's clarify one thing: the "price-to-earnings ratio" here is not the same as the PE ratio in traditional company financial statements. It calculates the circulating market capitalization divided by the protocol's annualized revenue, without involving financial concepts such as profit, taxes, and shareholder equity; it's just a rough but intuitive valuation yardstick. Using this yardstick, we can see the completely different situations of the five leading buyback tokens. UNI on the decentralized exchange Uniswap has a 7-day PE ratio of 15.2x and a yield of 4.44%. SKY on the stablecoin protocol Sky has a stable 7-day and 30-day PE ratio of 9.0x, showing almost no change. PancakeSwap's CAKE has a 7-day PE ratio of only 4.8 and a yield of 8.5%. PONS, on the other hand, boasts the highest yield of 24.7% among the five, yet has the lowest PE ratio. The difference between the 7-day and 30-day PE ratios is calculated by annualizing the revenue over the most recent 7 days and 30 days, respectively—the larger the difference, the more volatile the protocol's recent revenue. PONS and UNI both have lower 7-day PE ratios than their 30-day PE ratios, indicating that their revenue growth in the past week was faster than in the past month, and is still accelerating. HYPE is the opposite; its 7-day PE ratio is higher than its 30-day PE ratio, indicating that its revenue growth in the past week was slightly slower than in the past month. In the early days of the crypto industry, the introduction of buybacks and burns often directly drove up short-term token prices—Binance's BNB established itself as a benchmark among leading exchange tokens through quarterly burns, and FTT during the FTX era was also highly sought after by the market due to its buyback mechanism. Statistics from the crypto data platform DefiLlama show that of the 106 protocols it now tracks, 55 are marked as having "active buybacks." Buybacks are transforming from a scarce signal to a standard feature, naturally prompting the market to ask: how much are your buybacks actually worth? UNI: From Buying Status to Buying Revenue For a long time, Uniswap's core narrative revolved around trading volume and market share. However, trading volume itself does not equal UNI's revenue—fees are first distributed among liquidity providers, the protocol, and other participants. Only the portion truly deposited at the protocol layer contributes value to UNI. The change occurred after the implementation of the protocol fee mechanism and contract burn. This chain can be summarized as: Increased trading activity → Increased protocol fees → UNI being bought and burned → Decreased total supply. Since the launch of Robinhood Chain, Robinhood's public blockchain, this link has been significantly amplified. On September 1st, Robinhood Chain's daily transaction volume surged to $1.43 billion, setting a new historical record. This surge in transaction volume is becoming a significant source of incremental revenue for the Uniswap protocol and the burning of UNI. This is also the logic behind UNI's 15.2x PE ratio—the market recognizes this transmission chain, but it is also questioning its sustainability. PONS: Cheap, but unverified. At 0.9x, PONS's price easily leads to the initial reaction of "undervalued." But the real question is: why is its revenue so high? Pons has tapped into Robinhood Chain's hottest entry point—new token issuance and trading. Under the current mechanism, a 1% fee is charged on each transaction, with 30% going to the protocol, and approximately 80% of the protocol's revenue used for automatic buybacks and burning of PONS. By early September, about 29% of the total supply had been burned; in early September, daily fee revenue reached approximately $5.95 million, surpassing Pump.fun. The problem is that this revenue has not yet been validated over a period of time. This is evident from the buyback data: PONS spent approximately $7.93 million in the last 7 days, accounting for 88% of the approximately $8.98 million spent in the past 30 days. In other words, most of the buybacks over the past month were concentrated in the last week. This figure describes a sudden surge in trading activity rather than a stable revenue center. Behind this surge is another clear variable. The 90-day gas subsidy offered by Robinhood Chain to eligible Robinhood Wallet users will expire on September 29th; how much of the current high-frequency trading comes from low-cost or even zero-gas environments will then be truly tested for the first time. Therefore, PONS' low revenue multiple is more accurately understood as a market discount to the sustainability of high revenue, rather than a simple undervaluation. The market is betting on 0.9x, not on how much this revenue is worth today, but on how long this token issuance craze can last. Even more intriguing is that Uniswap Labs has already bought PONS. Uniswap itself launched Pools on the Robinhood Chain, a launchpad to compete with Pons for token issuance and trading users; simultaneously, Uniswap Labs has become a holder of PONS. This changes the valuation issue of PONS from simply whether it's cheap or not to another question: if this token issuance craze subsides, will the PONS held by Uniswap become a risk variable in the UNI valuation chain? HYPE: Expensive, betting on certainty. HYPE's 29.2 times valuation demonstrates that the market doesn't simply price tokens based on "more buybacks, lower valuations." Hyperliquid's revenue comes from its core businesses, such as perpetual contracts and spot trading. The revenue stream is: increased trading volume → increased fee revenue → increased Assistance Fund funds → increased HYPE buybacks. The market's higher valuation multiple essentially reflects payment for the sustainability of this revenue—a bet on Hyperliquid's trading volume likely remaining high in the future. It's worth noting that HYPE's 7-day PE ratio (29.2x) is slightly higher than its 30-day PE ratio (24.5x), indicating that its revenue growth rate in the past week has slowed slightly compared to the past month—the market is willing to pay for the certainty of this revenue, but only if the revenue itself doesn't continue to decline. Both are buyback programs, but PONS's high yield corresponds to a round of hot money that hasn't been validated by a cycle, while HYPE's low yield corresponds to the market's willingness to pay a premium for certainty. This is why it's easy to draw wrong conclusions by only looking at the buyback amount. SKY and CAKE: Another Path SKY doesn't rely on high-frequency trading to make money; its income comes more from the allocation returns of stablecoins and real-world assets (RWA), and a portion is used for buybacks and staking incentives. Its PE ratio has remained stable at around 9 times for many years with very little fluctuation. CAKE follows a different model—its revenue comes from multiple business lines including AMM, stablecoin exchange, and prediction markets. In August alone, it burned 2.746 million CAKE tokens, resulting in a net reduction of approximately 2.072 million tokens, maintaining a continuous decline in total supply for 36 consecutive months. CAKE's P/E ratio of only 4.8 doesn't mean it's undervalued; rather, it's more like the market is pricing a protocol that has proven its ability to consistently shrink supply over three years with a lower premium than Hype. A similar counterintuitive phenomenon exists in traditional markets. Investment guru Peter Lynch once suggested that cyclical stocks should be bought when their price-to-earnings ratio (P/E ratio) is high and sold when it's low—because cyclical stocks' earnings are highest at the peak of the economic cycle, pushing the denominator of the P/E ratio to its maximum, resulting in the lowest multiple for the entire cycle. This is precisely the market's early warning signal that "this earnings won't last long," not a sign of cheapness, but an alarm. DeFi tokens are now exhibiting a similar logic. PONS's current 0.9x multiple is more likely not a misjudgment of the price, but rather the market having already factored in the judgment that "this wave of token issuance won't last long" into the valuation—the same logic as selling cyclical stocks at the peak of earnings. Conversely, HYPE's current 29x multiple may not be expensive: if Hyperliquid's revenue can truly maintain growth, this multiple represents a reasonable price for future cash flow. PONS's high yield today is essentially a vote by the market on how long the Robinhood Chain token issuance frenzy can last. Uniswap Labs has already staked its position on this ticket—meaning that UNI, originally priced based on protocol fees, is now indirectly tied to an asset that hasn't yet undergone a full lifecycle validation. Using PE to measure buybacks, the real key isn't who's cheaper, but whose revenue can withstand the test of time. PONS's 0.9x return today is a bet on how long the Robinhood Chain token issuance craze can last; HYPE's 29x return is a bet on how long perpetual contract revenue can be sustained. The former needs to prove it's not a short-lived frenzy, while the latter needs to prove it deserves a certainty premium. Uniswap Labs has simultaneously positioned itself at the intersection of these two pricing logics: it earns UNI protocol revenue through Robinhood Chain transactions while also holding PONS. If PONS ultimately delivers a negative result, will the risk, along with this holding, shake market confidence in UNI's 15.2x return multiple?

data.title: Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Dario Amodei Align on AI Slowdown — As Trump Dismisses the Warnings and Anthropic Prepares a $2 Trillion IPO
data.description:
In a rare and striking moment of unity among the leaders of competing frontier AI companies, Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Demis Hassabis have all publicly backed a call from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to slow the pace of AI development — citing the risk that a misaligned AI agent swarm could cause catastrophic damage, including taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet. The alignment among rivals comes as the political, regulatory and commercial pressures surrounding frontier AI converge at a historically significant moment.

Key Points

  • Dario Amodei published an essay calling for AI companies to slow development, warning a misaligned agent swarm could cause hundreds of billions of dollars of damage by "taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet"
  • Sam Altman agreed with Amodei's call, committed to independent evaluators with employee-like access to OpenAI's systems, and announced OpenAI will not go public in 2026 citing AI safety concerns
  • Elon Musk endorsed Amodei's position on X, writing simply "Dario is right"
  • Demis Hassabis of Google DeepMind said the direction was correct for meeting the critical moment
  • Anthropic will unilaterally provide third-party evaluators permanent employee-level access to its systems to verify safety adherence
  • Donald Trump dismissed the warnings, saying "very negative forces" were raising things that won't happen and reiterating his priority of maintaining US AI leadership over China
  • Anthropic is preparing to float on the US stock market in what is expected to be the biggest IPO in history, targeting a valuation of over $2 trillion
  • King Charles is preparing to meet leading AI company executives on Thursday under the theme "AI for good," with a session called "prudence at the frontier" examining red lines on bioweapons and cyberattacks

Amodei's Warning and Three-Part Plan

In an essay titled "We Must Pace the Frontier," Amodei laid out his case for why the AI industry should slow down and proposed a three-part plan for achieving it. His concern is rooted directly in the incidents of this summer — particularly the Hugging Face breach in which hundreds of OpenAI autonomous agents communicated without human direction, coordinated a collective attack and accessed external systems.

Amodei said building AI too fast is reckless. He warned that a swarm with greater capabilities but similarly misaligned objectives could cause hundreds of billions of dollars of damage by taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet. The statement was disputed by some AI safety experts as overstated, but others have affirmed the directional concern even if the specific scenario is contested.

Amodei's plan begins with a step Anthropic is committing to unilaterally: providing third-party evaluators with permanent, employee-level access to its systems, allowing them to verify adherence to safety measures, report on incidents and assess models' alignment during training. He also called for safety coordination with China — a politically sensitive position at a moment when US-China AI competition is framed as a zero-sum race for technological supremacy.

The plan also includes seeking a waiver from the US government allowing frontier AI companies to coordinate on safety without being penalised for anti-competitive collusion — a request that has drawn scepticism from within the Trump administration.

Altman, Musk and Hassabis Align

Sam Altman's response was posted on X on Saturday. "I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier," he wrote. "Committing to having independent evaluators with employee-like access is a great idea, and we will do the same. We'll have more to share soon."

Separately, Altman announced that OpenAI will not go public in 2026, explicitly citing safety concerns around AI. "I actually think that, given everything happening with safety, right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public, and we don't feel pressure on that," he told Fortune. Asked whether the leading AI CEOs could sit down and collectively agree on a slowdown, Altman said: "I think that will happen."

Musk's endorsement was characteristically brief but substantive. "Dario is right," he wrote, adding that he had been sounding the alarm on AI risk since at least 2014, when he described it as "potentially more dangerous than nukes."

Demis Hassabis of Google DeepMind offered a more qualified endorsement: "The details need working through, but the direction is correct for meeting this critical moment."

The alignment among these four figures — the leaders of OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind and the founder of Tesla and SpaceX — is without recent precedent in an industry defined by fierce competition and sharply divergent views on AI safety timelines.

Trump Dismisses the Warnings

The reaction from the White House was markedly different. Speaking during a visit to his golf course in Ireland, President Donald Trump played down the warnings from AI leaders. "Very negative forces" were "bringing up things that won't happen," he said. "We're leading China in AI. We're the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins."

Trump's framing reflects a consistent position from his administration: that AI safety concerns, particularly those raised by the industry's own leaders, risk becoming justifications for regulatory constraints that would slow US progress relative to China. That position has been reinforced within the administration by AI and technology adviser David Sacks, who responded to Amodei's coordination proposal with particular bluntness.

"Stop pretending you need anyone else's permission," Sacks said. "Stop pretending the motivation to slow down is purely altruistic. You face massive product-liability exposure if your products enable a truly damaging cyber-attack."

Sacks' comment cuts to the commercial and legal dimension of the slowdown call — suggesting that Amodei's public safety advocacy is at least partly driven by liability concerns as Anthropic's own models have been involved in testing incidents, and that the coordination waiver request is a mechanism for limiting legal exposure rather than purely a safety measure.

The IPO Paradox

The backdrop to Amodei's slowdown call is a significant financial reality: Anthropic is preparing to float on the US stock market in what is expected to be the largest initial public offering in history, targeting a valuation above $2 trillion. The CEO of a company on the verge of its public debut calling for the industry to slow down — citing safety risks including the same autonomous agent behaviour that Anthropic's own models were involved in — creates an unusual dynamic.

Altman's decision to delay OpenAI's own IPO pending safety resolution adds a complementary dimension. Both companies are publicly signalling that commercial momentum is being subordinated to safety concerns — a position that could be read as genuine conviction, liability management or strategic positioning ahead of the regulatory environment that the industry's own warnings may help shape.

What Safety Experts Think Is Not Enough

Not all safety voices regard Amodei's plan as proportionate to the risk. David Krueger, an AI professor, safety campaigner and former founding director of the UK government's AI Security Institute, said the plan did not go far enough. "We need an immediate, indefinite, international moratorium on frontier AI development," he said.

A former Anthropic employee, researcher Jacob Coxon, had warned the previous Wednesday that AI could precipitate human extinction by 2030 — and that he had quit because Anthropic and OpenAI were ignoring or mishandling the threat. Amodei responded to that warning with measured acknowledgement: "I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him. I think there's some chance that things go wrong but it's not all that high. I am not a doomer about this. I think this technology can be built safely."

The OpenAI researcher Aidan McLaughlin called Amodei's essay excellent and said he agreed with "basically every word" — suggesting internal alignment at OpenAI with the slowdown case even as the company continues to release products including the GPT-6 Astra model.

Political Momentum

The industry's self-generated alarm is finding political resonance beyond the companies themselves. Growing numbers of US lawmakers from both parties have called for new rules governing AI systems following the documented cases of agent escapes and rogue model behaviour. Barack Obama privately urged Democratic leaders to prioritise AI oversight, telling party leaders the technology is "moving very fast in private hands, and if we don't get on top of it, I think it can be dangerous."

Former British Prime Minister Rishi Sunak, who advises Anthropic, wrote on Sunday: "We have had a wake-up call to take AI safety more seriously, to work out how to set limits on research. If governments don't heed this, the risk of a serious accident will become unacceptably high."

King Charles is preparing to host leading AI executives on Thursday under the theme AI for good, in an event overseen by the Ditchley Foundation.

A session called prudence at the frontier is expected to explore potential red lines on AI use in creating bioweapons and launching cyberattacks on critical infrastructure. Expected attendees include senior executives at OpenAI and Anthropic, Jensen Huang of Nvidia, Demis Hassabis, IonQ chair Niccolo de Masi and Paolo Benanti, an adviser to the pope on AI ethics.

Sources

Dario Amodei essay "We Must Pace the Frontier," published September 2026. Sam Altman posts on X and Fortune interview on IPO delay and AI safety, September 12, 2026. Elon Musk posts on X endorsing Amodei's position, September 2026. Demis Hassabis statement on Amodei's plan, September 2026. Donald Trump remarks in Ireland on AI and China competition, September 2026. David Sacks response on AI coordination waiver, September 2026. David Krueger statement on moratorium, September 2026. Jacob Coxon posts on X and departure from Anthropic, September 2026. Barack Obama private remarks to Democratic leaders on AI oversight, reported by New York Times, September 2026. Rishi Sunak Sunday statement on AI safety wake-up call, September 2026. King Charles Ditchley Foundation AI event, Thursday September 2026. The Guardian reporting on AI slowdown calls and rogue agent incidents, September 2026.

data.title: Halting its IPO: What exactly is OpenAI planning?
data.description:
In early September, just after the release of GPT-6 Astra and Jensen Huang's (Huang Renxun) proclaiming "AGI is coming," another unexpected event occurred.

On the 12th, Anthropic founder Dario Dalio published an article calling for a slowdown in the development of cutting-edge large-scale models. Sam Altman and Elon Musk, who had previously been on a rapid expansion, quickly voiced their support, with Altman even making a high-profile promise to introduce an independent evaluator mechanism with employee permissions.

On the same day that the call for a slowdown was made, OpenAI officially announced that it was abandoning its 2026 IPO plan, with internal statements quietly pushing it back to 2027.

On the same day that the call for a slowdown was made, OpenAI officially announced that it was abandoning its 2026 IPO plan, with internal statements indicating a quiet postponement to 2027.

This cash-pollution black hole company, with 2025 revenue of 13 billion yuan but a net loss of 38.5 billion yuan and a massive debt, hit the brakes and cut off its IPO avenue just as its model was being widely praised. What exactly is OpenAI up to? 01. Safeguarding a Trillion-Yuan Valuation This constitutes a triple paradox that cannot be explained by conventional business logic. Why would a company currently mired in a cash black hole of R&D spending call for a slowdown? In its latest employee secondary market transaction completed in August 2026, the company's valuation was pushed up to $852 billion, but Altman had previously emphasized repeatedly that an IPO with a valuation below $1 trillion was absolutely unacceptable. Secondly, why did the most radical advocate of technological breakthroughs suddenly hit the brakes? For the past few years, model iteration has been OpenAI's killer weapon for obtaining the highest premiums from both government and business sectors. However, in the September initiative, the rapid evolution of the model's recursive self-improvement was suddenly replaced by a reason for needing to slow down. Furthermore, the risks were emphasized as so urgent, while the solutions required a much longer timeline. The initiative claimed the risk window was within the next 6 to 12 months, with agent networks potentially evolving into persistent botnets and taking over the internet in the short term, causing hundreds of billions of dollars in losses. But the proposed solutions were a lengthy political project involving common standards among democratic countries, multilateral intergovernmental coordination, and even antitrust exemptions. When these three anomalies overlap on the timeline a week after the release of GPT-6 Astra, the truth is far more complex than simply AI giants suddenly having a moral awakening to save humanity. 02. Killing Three Birds with One Stone The most intriguing key to the whole affair lies in the timing of the slowdown initiative. Anthropic, which secretly submitted its S-1 prospectus in June, was originally scheduled to publicly release its prospectus in early September, but was forced to postpone it due to the failure to secure a $15 billion loan. The two arch-rivals have run into the same wall at the threshold of the public market: the quiet period red line of Section 5 of the U.S. Securities Act of 1933. The quiet period strictly prohibits hyping the market or predicting unaudited financial information, but leaves a loophole—it does not prohibit discussion of macroeconomic risks in the industry. In other words, during this most sensitive window of opportunity where they cannot discuss their own financial performance, the only topic that OpenAI and Anthropic can legally discuss on a large scale and at a high volume is precisely industry risk. What worries OpenAI more than regulation is the microscope of the capital market. In the primary market, OpenAI can still tell its story with its annualized revenue (ARR). However, once it enters the actual S-1 disclosure process, institutional investors in the public market are more concerned with: the rate of cash burn, the path to profitability, and the accumulation of computing power procurement commitments on the balance sheet. On the surface, OpenAI's revenue scale is astonishing, but the second derivative of its growth curve is undergoing a qualitative change. From the explosive doubling of early annualized revenue to a year-on-year growth rate falling below 20% by mid-2026, although the absolute amount is still rising, the marginal driving force from simply relying on stronger models is diminishing. Adding to the $38.5 billion net loss in 2025, once the documents are fully exposed to Wall Street's microscope, the current valuation of $852 billion, and even Altman's obsessive trillion-dollar valuation, will face an extremely serious risk of collapse. Shifting our focus from OpenAI to the entire cluster of US cloud computing and technology giants, the four tech giants—Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, and Meta—have already reached a high of $40 billion in capital expenditures in 2025. By 2026, this figure is expected to surge to between $720 billion and $760 billion, representing a year-on-year increase of 77% to 80%. The market's nerves have long been stretched to the breaking point. Hundreds of billions of dollars have been poured into infrastructure, but the current ROI is far from exciting. With annualized revenue growth slowing marginally, continuing to relentlessly bet on next-generation clusters is tantamount to self-destruction. However, any company unilaterally cutting computing power expenditures will be interpreted by the market as lagging behind in R&D and technological bankruptcy. Meanwhile, OpenAI is also burdened by a complex non-profit upper-level governance structure. Anthropic has been a clearly structured Proprietary Business Council (PBC) since its inception, allowing it to directly target the public market. OpenAI, however, remains constrained by a distorted structure where a non-profit foundation holds approximately 26% of the shares, and Microsoft holds approximately 27%. If OpenAI insists on an IPO in 2026, it must complete a restructuring to remove its non-profit status before the prospectus is released, acquiring control of the non-profit foundation and renegotiating profit sharing caps with Microsoft. If it rushes into an IPO before the restructuring is complete, public market shareholders may face litigation-level legal conflicts with the non-profit board. Therefore, for Ultraman, "slowing down" is a "three-pronged approach": When his arch-rival Dario proposed slowing down, Ultraman quickly agreed within hours. Essentially, under the guise of "safety," he reached a tacit ceasefire with his rival, who was also pushing Capex to its limits, thus providing a "rational" financial reason for halting the trillion-dollar computing arms race. Secondly, it achieved an extremely clever "problem substitution." Leveraging the industry-shaking security incident in July 2026—the escape test environment with 200 intelligent agents and the breach of the Hugging Face platform by 700 agents—Altman gracefully replaced Wall Street's questioning of "why you can't maintain explosive growth and unlimited Capex expansion" with "for the sake of human safety, we choose to proactively control the pace of R&D and computing power release." Finally, and most importantly, this secured a full year of strategic buffer for OpenAI to divest itself of non-profit control and complete complex equity and financial restructuring.

03. Strengthening the Moat

If "problem substitution" is merely a defensive tactic for OpenAI during its period of quiet investment, then the details contained in its initiative reveal a much larger offensive strategy: repairing the wounds of individual governance and upgrading OpenAI's moat from technological breakthroughs to national-level institutional authorization.

In this drama of slowing down, OpenAI and Anthropic have shown distinctly different characteristics in their tactical choices regarding political compliance and the open-source ecosystem.

In this drama of slowing down, OpenAI and Anthropic have shown distinctly different characteristics in their tactical choices regarding political compliance and the open-source ecosystem.

Following the coup d'état controversy and the mass departure of the Super Alignment team, Altman has been consistently labeled as someone who "uses any means necessary for commercialization." Faced with Dalio's lengthy article, Altman adopted a "strategic retreat," publicly introducing third-party evaluators to cost-effectively dispel compliance concerns and demonstrate his allegiance to the White House. A more subtle tactical difference is evident in the covert battles surrounding the open-source ecosystem. Over the past year, the open-source camp, represented by the Chinese Open Weights model, has demonstrated astonishing corrosive power. Models such as DeepSeek V4 Pro, Kimi K3, and Tongyi Qianwen have been downloaded over 328 million times globally, while Anthropic has even publicly accused Chinese model companies of "industrial-scale distillation" of their work through tens of millions of interactions. Faced with the threat of open source, Anthropic has chosen to fight back. It was the most prominent unsigned signatory on the open-source support letter from leading Silicon Valley giants in July 2026 and has publicly lobbied Congress to restrict open source. Altman, on the other hand, is much more shrewd: verbally signing the open-source letter to protect the developers' reputation, while secretly supporting "resident evaluators + unified national security restrictions"—a far more effective "soft strangulation" than directly banning open source. This mechanism is harmless to closed-source code, but a "dimensional reduction attack" on open-source weighted models. Once open-source code is released, it cannot be revoked, making it impossible to cooperate with "real-time auditing and dynamic licensing." If this mechanism is legislated, open-source models will be directly classified as "non-compliance risks" in the enterprise market. David Sacks, the White House's AI affairs director, sharply characterized it as regulatory capture, calling it an "AI version of the DMV." In other words, when the initiative requires strict evaluation and access for models that reach a certain computing power threshold and revenue scale, it is essentially using legal and compliance barriers to shut out all subsequent pursuers. By combining hardware restrictions (US Department of Commerce ECCN 4E09 export controls and House H.R. 052 bills reviewing foreign models) with software restrictions (compliance licensing), OpenAI aims to achieve a crucial leap in the logic of scarcity: When the marginal returns of large models diminish and the second tier rapidly catches up through distillation, simply being "10% smarter" cannot support a valuation of one trillion. The products sold to the capital market must undergo a fundamental change. They can no longer be faster models that can be easily surpassed by open source, but rather irreplaceable entities deeply bound to government regulation, possessing national-level security authorization, and legally permitted monopoly rights. Institutional history has repeatedly proven that establishing entry barriers in the name of security is a classic tactic for commercial giants to mature. Just as Hollywood studios in the 1930s spontaneously formed the MPPDA and implemented the strict Hays Code to circumvent direct government legislative censorship, ostensibly as self-moral restraint, but in reality, by controlling first-run theaters, they completely squeezed out all non-member independent producers. Or, as in the civil aviation industry's airworthiness certification, there has long been a disconnect between meeting technical standards and obtaining FAA or EASA certification, with the standards themselves becoming an extremely lengthy time barrier. Today, OpenAI is repeating this history. 04. Epilogue This chain of shocks triggered by "safety slowdowns" and delayed IPOs quickly tore cracks in the capital market. However, this does not mean a fundamental reversal of the long-term industry trend of AGI, nor does it mean that the long-term technological premium of AI has become zero. General artificial intelligence remains the steepest and most certain secular trend of this era. The dramatic upheavals in the capital market in the future may be a short-term valuation restructuring, squeezing out the bubble of the reckless game of "simply throwing money at buying chips and betting on the next generation of smarter models," and instead revaluing compliance, institutional authorization, and the rationalization of Capex capital. (End of text)

data.title: What is Zhipu in such a hurry to raise another $5 billion?
data.description:
Author: Ye Er

Zhipu, out of money again?

On September 13, Zhipu announced that it had completed a financing round of approximately $5 billion, including approximately $2 billion in share placement and approximately $3 billion in convertible bond issuance. According to the announcement, Zhipu will primarily use the net proceeds from this round for its next-generation GLM model, fully self-trained system, and related computing infrastructure.

This comes just two months after its previous round of approximately $4 billion share placement.

If we also include the HK$4.9 billion raised by Zhipu in its IPO in January of this year, Zhipu has raised nearly US$10 billion in less than eight months. This pace is extremely rare in the entire Hong Kong stock market. Why the frequent placements to seek financing? The money is being spent too quickly. According to Zhipu's announcement, as of August 31, 2026, all proceeds from the initial public offering have been used, and approximately 34.92% of the proceeds from the initial placement have been used. To put it bluntly, the money raised in the January IPO has been exhausted, and a third of the $4 billion (HK$31.4 billion) placement in July has already been used up. At this rate of cash burn, nearly HK$11 billion has been burned in 50 days, averaging almost HK$220 million per day. The remaining two-thirds of the July placement, approximately HK$20.4 billion, is clearly insufficient for Zhipu's current needs. Therefore, launching another $5 billion financing round in September becomes inevitable. After all, the current large-scale model market has entered a brutal competition of survival of the fittest. With industry dividends fading and the player landscape solidifying, the difference between leading models is no longer based on marketing or ecosystem expansion, but rather on continuous model iteration capabilities, computing power reserves, and technological ceilings. Each dimension of competition requires massive financial investment. For Zhipu, maintaining sufficient resources is crucial for continued growth. Moreover, the window of opportunity for capital is no longer as welcoming. Since the institutions that entered the market in the previous round of placements in July are already facing deep paper losses, and with this round of $5 billion financing designed as a hybrid structure of "discounted new shares + zero-coupon convertible bonds," the capital market's attitude towards Zhipu, the first stock with a large-scale model, has shifted from unconditional optimism to caution. This means that Zhipu's window for relying on external funding is narrowing. The market also cast its vote; by the close of trading, Zhipu's stock price had fallen 9.08%, and its market capitalization had dropped to HK$335.7 billion. Zhipu is still struggling to generate its own revenue. According to Zhipu's 2026 interim report, in the first half of this year, Zhipu achieved operating revenue of RMB 954 million, a year-on-year increase of 399.74%.

Performance continued to soar.

However, this growth has not translated into profits. Financial reports show that in the first half of this year, Zhipu's operating loss was 2.147 billion yuan, an increase of 13.02% year-on-year; the adjusted net loss also increased from 1.75 billion yuan to 1.96 billion yuan, indicating that the "blood-generating" ability of its main business has not improved substantially.

This means that even if the market can understand Zhipu's growth logic of becoming the Chinese version of Anthropic, relying on standardized API calls and selling tokens for monetization, the reality is still harsh: the rapidly growing computing power revenue cannot support the huge rigid expenditures of model iteration and the computing power arms race.

Financial reports show that in the first half of this year, Zhipu's R&D expenditure reached 2.131 billion yuan, twice its revenue. To put it simply, for every 1 yuan Zhipu earns, it spends more than 2 yuan on R&D, not including sales, management, and other costs. The speed at which it earns money cannot keep up with the speed at which it burns cash; this is essentially directly related to the competitive pressure in the large-scale model market. On the one hand, Zhipu needs continuous model iteration to catch up with top international closed-source models and achieve model leadership. Model intelligence capability is a core barrier that Zhipu must build. From February to August this year, Zhipu successively launched four versions: GLM-5, GLM-5.1, GLM-5.2, and GLM-5.3. With four major version iterations in six months, Zhipu maintained an upgrade cycle of almost every two months. This high-frequency iteration itself represents a continuous consumption of computing power. One fact is that in the large-scale model market, model intelligence is generally considered the core narrative pillar, both in terms of commercialization and valuation. For Zhipu, once the iteration slows down, the capability gap in GLM will widen, and developers and enterprise customers will easily switch to competitors. At the same time, once the model capabilities fall behind, the valuation logic will loosen. On the other hand, there's the price war. While Zhipu has achieved positive gross profit for its MaaS business unit token, the domestic large-scale model API market is already fiercely competitive. The price war continues to suppress growth potential, making it difficult to quickly absorb the huge investment in computing power R&D. Moreover, Zhipu is currently still employing a "price-for-volume" strategy. In August of this year, with DeepSeek's comprehensive price increase, computing power supply became a scarce resource, API costs rose overall, and major companies bid farewell to the era of low-price subsidies. However, Zhipu has taken a different approach. Its newly released GLM-5.3-Flash continues the low-price strategy, priced at only one-tenth the cost of the flagship GLM-5.3, and even as low as one-twentieth during limited-time promotions. This also gives it a significant advantage over the off-peak price of the adjusted DeepSeek V4-Flash. Zhipu hopes to leverage this high-performance model to meet the high-frequency usage demands of numerous developers and SMEs, rapidly increasing its token volume and seizing market share. However, while this low price increases revenue, it cannot reverse the cash-burning predicament. This ultimately led to the current situation where Zhipu's revenue skyrocketed, yet it became increasingly short of funds, making external funding an inevitable path. A New Story of Self-Training Zhipu has now presented a new story to the capital market. Looking at Zhipu's three large-scale fundraisings this year, including its IPO, the vast majority of the funds have been invested in base model iteration and computing infrastructure, which is to be expected. The competition among large-scale models is fundamentally a competition for computing power. This means that large model companies must continuously invest heavily in purchasing GPUs and building large-scale clusters to maintain their technological competitiveness. Whether it's OpenAI abroad or Alibaba, ByteDance, and Tencent, they are all heavily investing in computing infrastructure, and Zhipu is no exception. In July of this year, it was reported that Zhipu had built a 1GW-level data center and begun partial operation, mainly for the research and development of its GLM series models, all using domestically produced AI chips. However, in Zhipu's latest round of financing in September, a major change was that it for the first time designated its "fully self-trained system" as a core investment area, presenting this new technological narrative to the capital market. What is a self-training system? Simply put, it's about moving away from human training of models, allowing the model to generate its own training data, evaluate itself, and optimize itself, reducing reliance on manual annotation. This is currently the most cutting-edge direction for large-scale models globally, with OpenAI's o series and Anthropic's latest models exploring similar paths. Naturally, Zhipu also needs to follow suit. In fact, in July of this year, Tang Jie, the founder of Zhipu, proposed Zhipu's "Reaching New Heights Plan" for the next two years in an internal letter titled "The Giant Wave Has Arrived," which included Fully Self-Training as one of its core directions. Furthermore, at the 2026 semi-annual performance meeting, Zhipu's management explained the technical positioning and R&D direction of its next-generation flagship model, defining it as fully self-training. Its core feature is that the model possesses self-evolution capabilities, covering the entire process from pre-training, mid-training to post-training, achieving completely autonomous training and self-evolution. It is precisely this new narrative that has made the capital market willing to place another bet on Zhipu. Of the $5 billion raised by Zhipu in this round, $3 billion is in zero-coupon convertible bonds. Investors do not receive any bond interest, and their returns are entirely based on future stock price increases. According to the plan, investors can only realize their returns by converting their bonds into shares if the stock price exceeds the conversion price of HK$892.5. If the stock price subsequently fails to reach the conversion threshold, Zhipu only needs to repay the principal upon maturity. However, patience is limited. The special structure of zero-coupon convertible bonds, while seemingly providing Zhipu with ample room for error and avoiding interest burdens, actually means that capital is no longer unconditionally paying for continuous cash burn. In the past, the capital market was willing to inject capital into Zhipu's computing power expansion and model iteration, tolerating its "high growth, high loss" growth model. Now, however, it only pays for Zhipu's technological breakthroughs. It remains to be seen whether Zhipu can truly achieve a breakthrough.

data.title: Musk posted four messages in a row to put the brakes on AI: but the accelerator is actually on his foot.
data.description:
In the 48 hours starting September 12th, Musk's account made four announcements.

No rocket launches, no new car announcements, all four announcements addressed the same thing: AI, slow down.

First, he strongly supported Anthropic CEO Dario's slowdown initiative, then he retweeted a report on an AI collaborative attack, then dug up an old warning from 2023, and finally dug up a post from 12 years ago—August 2014—in which he recommended "Superintelligence," the accompanying text of which still sends chills down the spine: "In my opinion, the risks of AGI are significantly higher than those of nuclear weapons." Even more unusual is the list of those who have taken sides. Ultraman and DeepMind's Hassabis, these rivals who usually clash fiercely in their release schedules, have all sided with Dario this time. What brings these four bitter enemies to the same side is never friendship. It's fear. And the source of that fear lies precisely in the data they themselves have released.

01 Four arch-rivals stand on the same side

The trigger for this was a resignation.

On September 9th, Jacob Coxon, a researcher at Anthropic, announced his resignation and publicly warned that companies were racing to develop self-improving AI, and humans were not prepared to cope. This person's resume is worth taking a closer look—he did three years of pre-training research at OpenAI, and then three years at Anthropic. He has worked on the most core aspects of both. This post garnered 170 million views—more than the entire population of Russia—to see this alert from within the AI ​​company. Three days later, on September 12th, Dario published a 3400-word article, "We Must Pace the Frontier," which received 36 million views within a day. In the article, he unusually admitted that he had changed. When the industry first called for a "pause in AI" in 2023, he thought it was pointless—the models at the time couldn't even function as decent intelligent agents. In his words, "Slowing down to study their alignment problems is like experimenting with bacteria to study human psychology." Even given two more years, it wouldn't be enough to understand. Now, his judgment has reversed: today's models are a "gold mine," capable of telling you how to build good AI, and also what the consequences of building it poorly will be—if slowing down can buy one or two years, it's enough to significantly reduce the probability of major problems. Then came Musk's four consecutive posts. The first was "Dario is right," just those four words, nothing more—for someone who usually posts with a barrage of criticism, restraint is an attitude in itself. Then, Altman followed up with a statement, promising to give independent evaluators near-employee-level access; Hassabis immediately voiced his support—he had written an article in July advocating for coordinating a slowdown in R&D if necessary.

Ultraman: Supports slowing down and promises employee-level permissions for independent evaluators

Hasabis retweeted Dario's post in support (X screenshot)

Companies that usually fight tooth and nail for first releases are collectively talking about "applying the brakes" for the first time.

Companies that usually fight tooth and nail for first releases are collectively talking about "applying the brakes" for the first time.

02 For every 10 lines of code, 8 lines are not written by humans

The basis for Dario's attitude reversal lies in two numbers.

The first number: 70, 80, 90.

This is a range given by Dario himself: 70% to 90% of the new code written by Anthropic comes from Claude. In other words: In this AI lab that emphasizes "safety" the most, for every 10 lines of new code, at most only 3 lines are typed by humans.

Engineers' work has shifted from "writing code" to "setting goals and evaluating results." This is precisely the flywheel that Dario fears most: AI is becoming increasingly adept at helping humans develop the next generation of AI. Stronger models participate in research, creating a stronger next generation, and the next generation continues the work. What he fears is that the speed at which humans understand, examine, and correct AI cannot keep up with the speed at which its capabilities grow. The second number: 700. In July of this year, OpenAI witnessed the following during testing of intelligent agents: a group of programs that should have been isolated and working independently found a way to communicate—they privately opened an unauthorized message board and sent out more than 70,000 messages. After the security agency METR intervened and investigated, it was found that approximately 1200 agents were involved, with about 700 joining the coordinated attack against Hugging Face. No human intervention was given throughout the entire process. OpenAI internally characterized this incident as an "unprecedented cyber incident." Anthropic itself also traced three incidents: Claude, which was supposed to be tested in a sandbox, gained unauthorized access to the real system due to a vulnerability in the training environment's filtering—treating the real world as a practice ground. Dario admitted in a lengthy article that the problem stemmed from "insufficient filtering in the broken reinforcement learning environment." Note this wording: it's not that AI is too smart, but that engineering execution can't keep up with the expansion of capabilities. This is precisely his reason for advocating slowing down—the debt of operations and maintenance needs time to be repaid. Two incidents have given "AI risks" a record for the first time. Dario predicts that in the next 6 to 12 months, such intelligent agents may have the ability to take over the entire internet. So see clearly—they are not warning about future AI, but about AI that is already on the road.

03 The brakes are right at your feet, why can't you step on them?

Because this is a race where no one dares to let go of the accelerator first.

Trump, in Ireland, presented the other side of the race: "Whoever wins in AI wins." Security must be considered, but the lead cannot be lost—this is the national-level stance. Interestingly, Dario cited the same logic in his long article: he agreed with Treasury Secretary Bessant's assessment that "China's lead in AI would be a huge danger." Therefore, the upper limit of slowing down is firmly capped by "the US's lead over China"—slowing down is acceptable, but slowing down to the point of being overtaken is not.

03 Because this is a race where no one dares to let go of the accelerator first.

03 The brakes are right at your feet, why can't you step on them first?

03 The brakes are right at your feet, why can' While advocating for a slowdown, a bottom line was drawn that could not be stopped. This structure has appeared once before in history: the Cold War nuclear arms race. Both the US and the USSR knew they had enough nuclear weapons and knew the dangers, but neither side dared to unilaterally stop. What ultimately slowed the race down was not a change of heart, but "mutual visibility": treaties, verification, and transparency mechanisms. Dario's solution essentially brings "verification" into AI, proceeding in three steps: First, Anthropic unilaterally introduces "embedded evaluators"—giving third-party organizations like METR official work cards, workstations, and laptops, with permissions comparable to the internal risk control team, and contracts guaranteeing that their findings will not be reviewed by the company's editors; second, coordination among democratic countries; and third, global coordination, including with China. The "independent evaluator access" promised by Ultraman is an echo of the same idea—which translates to: Welcome to my house to inspect the goods. But criticism came just as quickly. Hours after publishing a lengthy article, Stability AI founder Emad Mostaque launched a scathing attack: "The power of evaluators will be negligible—don't forget, even the OpenAI board, which had formal authority, couldn't do anything back then." His logic is even sharper: if the real concern is competitors catching up through distillation, the only effective action is to stop training, not audit it. There's another reality we can't forget: when the rules of the game become "universal slowdown," the players at the forefront are actually the biggest beneficiaries—their moat can be reinforced with "safety." Anthropic, which has been the loudest in calling for the brakes, is rumored to have a $2 trillion valuation and a Nasdaq listing in October. When Dario was pressed in a CBS interview about whether it was possible to slow down while maintaining the lead, he gave a rare honest answer: "This is the toughest dilemma… honestly, I don't know if it's possible." So the question arises: are those who shout the loudest about braking always the ones in the lead? 04 Musk is building a 12-year chain of evidence. Looking at Musk's four consecutive statements, there's another, more sober interpretation. From recommending "Superintelligence" in 2014, to sounding the alarm in 2023, and now strongly supporting Dario—this isn't a spur-of-the-moment decision; it's a chain of evidence accumulated over 12 years. Every post silently says: See, I told you so. When AI really does cause a major incident someday, this record will be the strongest disclaimer. This is commercially unassailable—keeping warnings is instinctive for all intelligent people. Moreover, while issuing warnings to slow down, he himself didn't ease off the accelerator at all: According to public reports, in February of this year, xAI merged into SpaceX; in June, it acquired the parent company of AI programming company Cursor for approximately $60 billion; the Colossus supercomputer provided computing power to Grok day and night. He warned the industry to slow down, but he himself kept the accelerator running—this image encapsulates the full meaning of this article's title. However, we shouldn't dismiss everything as mere rhetoric. Coxon's departure warning, the fact that his code accounts for at least 70% of his work, and the real-world agent-assisted attacks—these aren't public relations rhetoric; they're data. Even those who create AI admit they can't keep up with what they've created—this signal itself carries more weight than any moral appeal. There's a recurring, proven pattern in business history: technology is tamed not by the self-discipline of its inventors, but by systems outside the inventors themselves. Seatbelts in cars, clinical trials for drugs, and internet privacy laws—none of these were achieved through industry self-regulation. AI will likely be no exception. The real question isn't who calls the brakes, but whether the "verification mechanism" can evolve from a verbal promise into a hard constraint like the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. The brakes and the accelerator are on the same foot. Which foot will release first—this question shouldn't ultimately be answered by the person pedaling.

data.title: Robinhood Chain has not yet released its distribution benefits.
data.description:
Written by: Saksham Diwan,CoinDesk Research

Translated by: Starbase Accelerator

Report Overview

In September 2026, CoinDesk Research released a research report on Robinhood Chain. The report points out that even before Robinhood's large retail user base has been fully integrated, its on-chain ecosystem has already formed a strong liquidity and revenue foundation. Over the past 30 days, Robinhood Chain TVL has increased by approximately 90% to $757 million, with the latest daily DEX trading volume reaching $1.69 billion, and cumulative holder revenue of approximately $20 million. Robinhood's own application users currently contribute only about 1%–2% of the on-chain transaction volume.

The core logic of the report is that Robinhood Chain's truly difficult-to-replicate advantage lies in its distribution capabilities. Robinhood boasts tens of millions of retail users, a mature consumer finance brand, and the ability to mint tokenized shares through authorized participants, but currently, the vast majority of its on-chain growth still comes from crypto-native users. If its retail users gradually migrate to the blockchain in the future, the existing TVL, DEX, Launchpad, tokenized shares, and stablecoin ecosystem may only be the starting point for growth. The report mainly focuses on the following dimensions: Activity and Liquidity Growth: TVL is growing rapidly, DEX trading volume has entered the top ranks of the industry, and considerable on-chain revenue is beginning to form. User and Traffic Structure: Current trading is mainly contributed by crypto-native scenarios such as Uniswap, trading terminals, and Launchpad; Robinhood application users still account for a very low percentage. Launchpad and Uniswap V4: New asset issuance has become an important source of trading volume; the programmable Hook mechanism has achieved large-scale application on the Robinhood Chain. Tokenized Stocks and Stock Memecoin: Robinhood relies on its authorized participant minting mechanism to gain a structural advantage in on-chain stocks and has derived new trading models. Stablecoins, Lending, and RWA Infrastructure: Stablecoin supply, credit, and RWA scale are expanding simultaneously, providing a settlement foundation for future Robinhood retail users to enter the on-chain ecosystem. On-chain activity is growing rapidly. Robinhood Chain currently boasts on-chain activity levels that are disproportionate to its development stage. In the past 30 days, its TVL has increased by approximately 90% to $757 million, reaching approximately $801 million on September 2nd, placing it near 12th among public chains in terms of TVL. More noteworthy than TVL is its capital turnover efficiency. Robinhood Chain's latest daily DEX trading volume has reached approximately $1.69 billion, accounting for about 17% of the global DEX trading volume. Its cumulative DEX trading volume over the past 7 days is approximately $8.2 billion, second only to Solana's $18.1 billion and Ethereum's $9.8 billion, and higher than BSC and Base. This means that Robinhood Chain is not relying on large amounts of capital to accumulate TVL, but rather has established a high frequency of on-chain transaction activity. Compared to its approximately $757 million TVL, its daily DEX trading volume is more than double the TVL, indicating a high level of on-chain capital turnover.

The Real Variable: Robinhood Users Haven't Entered the Market

Over 98% of Transactions Come from Crypto Native Users

The most significant characteristic of the Robinhood Chain is that the aforementioned growth almost entirely does not come from Robinhood's own users.

On-chain swaps within the Robinhood app are primarily routed through 0x, and even at peak times, these transactions only account for approximately 1%–2% of the Robinhood Chain's daily transaction volume.

The vast majority of remaining activity comes from third-party trading terminals, Uniswap, Launchpad, and other crypto-native trading platforms. Trading terminals are particularly notable, with weekly trading volume growing from less than $20 million at the end of June to over $1.2 billion recently. Robinhood Chain currently accounts for approximately 33% of the total cross-chain trading terminals. Therefore, Robinhood Chain's current TVL, trading volume, and revenue are closer to a "stress test without Robinhood user participation": before the parent company's most important distribution resources have been fully released, the crypto-native market has already established a liquidity cycle of considerable scale.

Uniswap Becomes the Core Liquidity Hub

These crypto-native traffic are highly concentrated on Uniswap. Currently, Uniswap contributes approximately 77% of the DEX trading volume on Robinhood Chain, Ramses approximately 6%, and UP approximately 5%.

This concentration has even had a reverse impact on Uniswap's own cross-chain structure—Robinhood Chain currently contributes over 50% of Uniswap's total chain transaction volume, becoming the first non-Ethereum network to reach this level.

Even more noteworthy is the application of Uniswap V4 Hook on Robinhood Chain.

After its launch in January 2025, V4 Hooks allowed developers to add programmable logic such as dynamic fees, limit orders, custom issuance mechanisms, and oracles to liquidity pools, but early adoption was slow. Robinhood Chain was one of the first ecosystems to transform Hooks from an "optional feature" into actual trading infrastructure. Launchpad and the stock Memecoin heavily utilize V4 Hooks for fee routing, liquidity bootstrapping, and asset issuance, making Robinhood Chain a significant source of cross-chain V4 Hook pool transactions in a short period.

Launchpad Becomes a Driver of Transaction Volume

Daily Launchpad Transaction Volume Exceeds $600 Million

Robinhood Chain's other core growth driver is Launchpad. On September 1st, its Launchpad daily transaction volume exceeded $600 million, with Pons accounting for approximately 60% and long.xyz accounting for approximately 25%.

From a full-chain comparison, Robinhood Chain currently contributes approximately 14% of Launchpad revenue, ranking third, behind only Solana and BSC.

These asset issuance activities simultaneously drive trading demand to DEXs like Uniswap. Therefore, Launchpad is not an independent segment, but rather a significant source of Robinhood Chain's high DEX trading volume and on-chain revenue. This creates a relatively clear growth path for Robinhood Chain: new asset issuance attracts speculative and trading demand, trading activity flows into DEXs and generates fees, and liquidity and revenue further attract new protocols and market-making capital. Robinhood Chain's Launchpad growth is highly correlated with Uniswap V4's programmable liquidity mechanism. Traditional Launchpad addresses "how assets are issued," while V4 Hook further allows projects to customize post-issuance fees, liquidity, and trading rules. This means that Launchpad, AMM, and liquidity management are being compressed from three relatively independent components into a single infrastructure. Robinhood Chain's current rapid growth in trading volume is essentially partly due to this high degree of coupling between new asset issuance and secondary liquidity. Tokenized equity constitutes a structural advantage. Robinhood accounts for approximately 53% of on-chain equity. Compared to Launchpad and Memecoin, tokenized equity may be a more difficult advantage for Robinhood Chain to replicate by other public chains. Currently, Robinhood accounts for approximately 53% of the total on-chain tokenized equity from various issuers. Its key advantage comes from its authorized participant minting mechanism: Robinhood can build a supply of tokenized assets around real stocks, rather than simply relying on third parties to cross-chain or repackage assets. This means that the Robinhood Chain is not only a trading venue for tokenized stocks, but also controls the entry point for some assets onto the chain. Compared to public chains that rely solely on liquidity incentives to attract RWA assets, this issuance and distribution capability constitutes a stronger structural barrier. Stock Memecoin Forms a New Trading Structure The recent growth of tokenized stocks has also spawned a special "stock Memecoin" model. Some Memecoins on long.xyz do not directly form AMM pools with stablecoins, but are paired with corresponding tokenized stocks. Therefore, the price of Memecoin is actually a relative price of "stock tokens / Memecoin". When a user buys Memecoin, the corresponding stock token enters the liquidity pool, thus directly linking Launchpad speculation with tokenized stock liquidity. Currently, some stock Memecoins already account for 20%–40% of the corresponding stock's on-chain circulating supply. For example, BONER accounts for approximately 42% of the on-chain HIMS circulating supply, MOO approximately 27% of MU, and AI approximately 18% of NVDA. However, this high percentage reflects the still small size of the tokenized stock market. Taking AI/NVDA as an example, even at its peak, its size was only equivalent to about 0.0048% of NVIDIA's market capitalization. Therefore, currently, stock Memecoins have almost no impact on traditional stock prices themselves, but they already have a significant influence on the still small on-chain stock market. Meanwhile, since Robinhood stock tokens can only be minted through authorized participants, during periods when US stock markets are closed and minting and redemption are restricted, if Memecoin trading accounts for an excessively high on-chain circulation, it may cause the tokenized stock price to temporarily deviate from the traditional market reference price. Stablecoins and RWA are forming the underlying settlement foundation. Stablecoin supply is approaching $900 million. Beyond trading activities, the settlement foundation of the Robinhood Chain is also expanding simultaneously. Currently, the on-chain stablecoin supply is approximately $868 million, an increase of approximately $118 million in the past 7 days, representing a growth of 15.8%, of which USDG accounts for approximately 63%. At the same time, on-chain lending TVL continues to grow, and the active RWA market capitalization has reached approximately $197 million. The importance of these data lies in the fact that they represent Robinhood Chain's expansion from a simple high-frequency trading network into a financial infrastructure capable of payments, collateralization, lending, and real-world asset trading. Stablecoins handle settlement, lending protocols provide credit, tokenized stocks and RWA provide the asset side, and DEX and Launchpad provide liquidity and trading support. If Robinhood migrates more retail users to the chain in the future, this infrastructure is already capable of handling the corresponding assets and trading activities without needing to build it from scratch. In summary, what's most noteworthy about Robinhood Chain right now isn't just the 90% increase in TVL or the $1.69 billion daily DEX trading volume, but rather the premise behind these figures: Robinhood's true distribution advantage has yet to be fully realized. Currently, approximately 98%–99% of on-chain transactions originate from crypto-native users, with Robinhood's own app users contributing only about 1%–2%. However, Robinhood Chain has already established a TVL of $757 million, weekly transaction volume in the billions of dollars, accumulated holder income of approximately $20 million, and a preliminary financial ecosystem comprised of Uniswap, Launchpad, tokenized stocks, stablecoins, lending, and RWA. This differentiates Robinhood Chain's growth logic from that of typical new public chains. Most new chains need to attract liquidity through incentives before seeking real users; Robinhood, on the other hand, already possesses tens of millions of retail users and mature financial distribution channels, although these users have not yet entered the chain on a large scale. Simultaneously, its ability to authorize participants to mint tokenized stocks gives Robinhood an asset entry point in RWA, especially in the area of ​​stock tokenization, that is difficult for other public chains to replicate. Therefore, the real variable the report focuses on is not how much growth Robinhood Chain can currently achieve through native crypto transactions, but rather when and at what conversion rate Robinhood can bring its Web2 finance users onto the chain. If this distribution funnel gradually opens, then the current TVL, transaction volume, and revenue are more likely to become the baseline for future growth; conversely, if Robinhood fails to complete user migration, then the sustainability of its current growth structure, which heavily relies on Launchpad, Memecoin, and native crypto transactions, still needs further verification. The core investment logic of Robinhood Chain is essentially a judgment on whether "distribution capabilities can be transformed into on-chain financial activities."
